title: House and Winter
premise: Petra Winterbourne, a skeptical urban explorer, maps an unmapped tunnel network beneath the drowned town of Harrow's Bend and finds a door sealed from the inside—behind it, the descendants of families who vanished in 1911, still counting their members for a harvest that comes every fifty years. As the excavation crew breaches deeper chambers, Petra realizes the family's survival depends on completing their count before the harvest moon rises, and that her own bloodline is on their ledger. She smuggles them out through the tunnels she knows better than anyone, but the house itself follows its people, and on the night of the moon Petra must choose between erasing her name from the ledger or taking her place in it. In the end she burns the ledger, freeing the family at the cost of her memories of belonging—and walks out of the tunnels unable to remember why she came.
about_author: Sable Almeida is the pen name of a former municipal surveyor who spent a decade mapping infrastructure beneath three midwestern cities before turning to fiction. They write horror about places that remember more than the people who built them.

chapters.title: The Survey Says Nothing
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. She maps storm drains beneath Harrow's Bend for a client's insurance audit and notices a tunnel branch absent from every survey since 1911. Her skepticism is established as armor; the emotional beat is the quiet thrill of being the only person who knows something the maps don't.

chapters.title: Crew Nineteen
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. The excavation crew hires her as a consultant after finding her unofficial maps online. She descends with them into the new branch, hiding how much she already knows. The beat is unease: the tunnel walls are brick where they should be bedrock, laid by hands, not water.

chapters.title: A Door Sealed From the Inside
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. The crew unearths an iron door bolted shut from within, its hinges oiled, its frame warm. Foreman Dade wants it opened; Petra argues to seal the shaft. The beat is dread disguised as professional disagreement—she touches the door and feels a pulse like a second heartbeat.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Counts
chapters.summary: Petra's POV, alone at night. Against her own advice she returns and slips through a maintenance gap behind the door. Inside: a preserved 1911 household, lamplit, occupied. A woman named Ilsa catches her and checks a ledger before speaking. The beat is vertigo—the impossible made domestic.

chapters.title: The Family Below
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Ilsa explains nothing but feeds her bread and shows her portraits of the vanished: forty-one names, including a Winterbourne. Petra denies any connection, but the family treats her as expected, almost overdue. The beat is the horror of being recognized by strangers.

chapters.title: Fifty Years Between Harvests
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. Flashback chapter: 1961, the last harvest moon, when the house took old Tomas and the family sealed the door again. Ilsa, then a girl, swore never to let the count come up short. The beat is grief hardened into ritual, and the first hint of what 'the count' demands.

chapters.title: Breach
chapters.summary: Dade's POV. The crew cuts the hinges. Light floods the under-house for the first time in decades, and the family scatters into inner rooms while Dade films everything for the client. The beat is violation—Petra watches from the dark, furious at herself for leading them here.

chapters.title: Names on the List
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. She steals a look at the ledger: forty-one entries, each closed with a date except one—WINTERBOURNE, P., left open, waiting. Above ground she researches her great-grandmother and finds a 1911 disappearance report she was never told about. The beat is denial cracking.

chapters.title: The Client Wants Access
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. The development firm plans a press event inside the 'historic discovery,' scheduling it—Petra realizes with cold clarity—for the night of the harvest moon. She warns Dade; he laughs. The beat is isolation: the only believer now is the one who never believed.

chapters.title: Ilsa's Bargain
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. Ilsa offers Petra a trade: help move the family out through the old drainage run before the moon rises, and the ledger will mark her line paid in full. But the house must not be left empty—if no one remains, it goes looking. The beat is a bargain struck in bad faith on both sides.

chapters.title: Mapping the Way Out
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. She spends two days charting an escape route through collapsed sections only she can read, marking passages with chalk while the family packs generations of belongings. The beat is reluctant tenderness—she begins to belong to them even as she plans their flight.

chapters.title: The Boy Who Waits at Doors
chapters.summary: Young Emeric's POV. The family's youngest has never seen the sky and keeps vigil at the breached door, talking to the crew above. Through him we see the family's captivity as inheritance, not imprisonment. The beat is heartbreaking innocence inside the horror.

chapters.title: Dade Goes Down Alone
chapters.summary: Dade's POV. Curious and greedy, Dade enters alone at night to photograph the ledger. He reads his own surname among the open entries—his family sold the crew contract, and the house noticed. The beat is a skeptic's conversion, too late and too loud; he runs, and the corridors rearrange behind him.

chapters.title: The House Wakes
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. With the moon two nights out, the house begins moving: doors migrate, staircases lengthen, the exit shaft seals itself with fresh brick. The family says this happens when the count nears. The beat is claustrophobia—the map she trusted becomes a liar.

chapters.title: Forty Open Names
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. Ilsa confesses the truth: the family didn't hide from the harvest—they feed it. Each cycle someone must stay, and the ledger keeps score. She chose Petra's line because a Winterbourne was owed. The beat is betrayal, and Petra understanding she was recruited, not rescued.

chapters.title: Chalk and Ash
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Petra tests whether the house obeys the ledger rather than the walls: she writes over an entry in chalk and a sealed corridor opens. The house is a machine of record-keeping. The beat is dawning strategy—she can't fight the house, but maybe she can falsify its books.

chapters.title: Evacuation
chapters.summary: Petra's POV, intercut with Emeric's. Under a false moonless sky forecast, Petra moves the family through the drainage run in shifts, carrying children past collapsing brick while the house groans and rewrites itself around them. The beat is desperate momentum—the plan working until it doesn't.

chapters.title: The Count Comes Up Short
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. One child, Emeric, is missing—drawn back by the open door. The harvest moon clears the ridge. Above, the press event lights flood the site. The beat is catastrophe: the family is out, but the ledger is one name short, and the house will collect from whoever holds the pen.

chapters.title: Harvest Moon
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. She goes back for Emeric as the house fully wakes, corridors breathing, portraits opening their eyes. She finds him at the threshold and carries him toward the light while the house offers her everything she's ever lacked—belonging, recognition, a name on a page. The beat is temptation at full voice.

chapters.title: The Burning
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. At the heart of the house, Petra tears the ledger free and burns it in the hearth that has burned since 1911. The house screams in brick and dust; the family outside feels chains lift. The beat is triumph purchased in advance—she knows the fire takes payment in memory.

chapters.title: Out Ahead of the Count
chapters.summary: Petra's POV, fraying. She walks Emeric out into the press-event floodlights as the house collapses inward, sealing itself forever. Rescuers ask who she is; she opens her mouth and finds the answer gone. The beat is bittersweet victory—everyone saved, including the girl who no longer knows she saved them.

chapters.title: House and Winter
chapters.summary: Epilogue, shifting between Ilsa and Petra. Months later, the family rebuilds above ground, keeping their rituals without the ledger, and quietly watch over Petra, who visits Harrow's Bend without knowing why. On her doorstep appears a blank book and a note: 'Some counts start over.' The beat is haunted hope—memory lost, belonging chosen anew.
